papers.title: Native FPGA Hard-Block Implementation from High-Level Synthesis
authors: Mohamed Bouaziz, Mahmoud A. Elshenawy, Krishnan B. Iyer, Abdurauf Abdurakhmanov, Ammar M. Seliaman, Suhaib A. Fahmy
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.25281v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-level synthesis (HLS) maps computations to FPGA hard blocks, yet often leaves their arithmetic modes, internal registers, and cascade links idle and recreates them in the fabric, costing area and timing. We present a C++ template library that reaches native hard-block implementations without modifying the HLS compiler. Templates fix source patterns, and an automatic flow picks scheduling settings and verified RTL patches. On AMD Versal, our matrix multiplication uses 2.4--4.5x fewer lookup tables (LUTs) than AutoSA systolic arrays at equal or higher estimated throughput. Our INT8 matrix--vector units reach the three multiply--accumulates per DSP of hand-written FINN RTL, versus at most 1.29 for HLS libraries. In hls4ml, Allo, and Stream

papers.title: Bottom-Up FPGA Reconfigurable Accelerator Overlay Generation
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.25293v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Programmable FPGA overlays run new workloads without re-synthesis, yet they pay twice. An overlay adds a second layer of programmability on top of the FPGA's own overhead. Moreover, overlay generators usually start from a regular template, so they spend logic on switches and links that the workloads never use, and they close timing at low clocks. We present a flow that instead grows an overlay bottom-up from the dataflow graphs of the workloads it must run. The flow clusters workloads by structural similarity, ranks shared slots with spectral descriptors of each operation's surroundings, and adds only the units and links a workload lacks. It builds every unit on native hard blocks, with their internal pipeline registers, dual-ported memories

papers.title: Flex-Plorer: A Precision-Aware Hardware-Software Co-Design Framework for an Edge SNN Accelerator
authors: Mohammad Farahani, Mohammad Rasoul Roshanshah, Saeed Safari
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2602.18140v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Neuromorphic accelerators promise high energy efficiency and computational density for spiking neural networks (SNNs), especially in wearable devices and neural prosthetics where power constraints are stringent. However, most existing platforms exhibit rigid architectures with limited configurability, which restricts their adaptability to heterogeneous signals and diverse design objectives. To address this gap, we present Flex-Plorer, a precision-aware hardware-software co-design framework using heuristic search over weight and decay precisions for a fixed architecture. It couples hardware-aware fixed-point simulation with synthesis-trained LUT/FF estimators and analytical BRAM estimation to guide user-defined accuracy-resource trade-off

papers.title: BROAD: Bit-Parallel Row-Oriented Arithmetic in DRAM
authors: William C. Tegge, Jo\~{a}o Paulo Cardoso de Lima, Shouzhi Fang, Jeronimo Castrillon, Alex K. Jones
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.02502v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Processing-using-memory (PUM) architectures perform computation directly within DRAM to reduce costly data movement between memory and processors. Because charge-sharing operations are confined to individual bitlines, existing DRAM-PUM architectures reorganize data into column-oriented, bit-serial representations. This organization is fundamentally incompatible with the row-oriented, word-parallel layouts used by conventional processors and accelerators, requiring expensive data-layout transformations whenever computation transitions between PUM and conventional execution. papers.title: TRANSIT: Transparent Scale-in for Multi-Node LLM Training
authors: Hyungyo Kim, Nicholas Satchanov, Hrishi Shah, Gaohan Ye, Jiaqi Lou, Robert Walkup, Shweta Salaria, I-Hsin Chung, Hubertus Franke, Seetharami Seelam, Apoorve Mohan, Nam Sung Kim
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.07593v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The growing memory requirements of large language models (LLMs) increasingly force distributed training jobs to span multiple GPU nodes to accommodate their training state. This reduces per-GPU computational efficiency, increases network traffic, and exacerbates job queueing delays. To address these inefficiencies, we introduce TRANSIT, a system that transparently enables efficient distributed LLM training on fewer GPUs through memory oversubscription. TRANSIT optimizes CPU-GPU data movement during oversubscription by coordinating driver-managed page residency with execution-guided zero-copy access, exploiting recurring kernel execution patterns across training iterations.
  We evaluate TRANSIT on dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE)

papers.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
authors: Arnab Sanyal, Gourav Datta, Sandeep P. Chinchali
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.17108v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Memory determines which large language models (LLMs) an edge device can run and how fast it runs them: capacity limits a 4 GB Jetson Nano, and bandwidth limits an 8 GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed weight formats (GPTQ, AWQ, and the GGUF K- and I-quants) spend the same number of bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. We present LazyWeights, which keeps these formats, tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes.
